questions.problem:
$$ A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ ${e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}} ${e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t)={e}^{-2t} \\ r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtraction the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-4t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}) \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2\cdot (-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-{e}^{4t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x,\,{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?
questions.worked_solution:
Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}=[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order.

questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=5t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ r(5t)={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ 5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{5{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{5t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2t\cdot \frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}}{3t}+\frac{5{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{5t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5t\cdot \frac{{e}^{5t}-{e}^{2t}}{3t}+\frac{5{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{5t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-t)={e}^{-t} \\ r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-t}}{3}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{-t} \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2\cdot \frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}

{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(5t)={e}^{5t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(5t)={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{5t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
5t{e}^{5t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}(1-5t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5{e}^{5t}t+{e}^{5t}(1-5t) \\  & ={e}^{5t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{5t}t \\  & =t{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].
$$
